To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Substance use disorders are prevalent among individuals with schizophrenia and are associated with poorer outcomes.

substance use disorder (SUD) treatment in schizophrenia is a complex problem, but that a better understanding of neurobiological mechanisms of treatment may be useful for developing new and more effective treatments.
substance use disorders (SUSDs) are highly prevaent among individuals with schizophrenia and that treatments for these disorders have been found to be more effective when integrated.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and evaluation of treatments for substance use disorders in patients with schizophrenia, and the neurobiological mechanism(s) that may underlie the effectiveness of such interventions.
the development of effective treatments for co-occurring SUDs in individuals with schizophrenia.
the development, evaluation, and dissemination of evidence-based treatments for SUD in schizophrenia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the neurobiological mechanism of the effectiveness of pharmacologic and psychologic treatments for substance use disorder in schizophrenia is not well understood, but that brain reward circuitry is an important target.
there is no single unifying mechanism for the development of SUDs in patients with schizophrenia, but that the most likely mechanism is the disruption of the brain's reward pathway.

effective pharmacologic and psychologic treatments for SUD in schizophrenia may work through modulation of reward circuit dysfunction, and that future studies should be aimed at understanding this mechanism in greater detail. (Contains 1 table and 1 figure.)
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

there is a need to better understand the mechanisms underlying the effectiveness and limitations of current treatment approaches for SUDs among individuals with schizophrenia, with a particular focus on the brain reward circuitry.

there is a neurobiological basis for the development of SUDs in individuals with schizophrenia, which is likely to be a shared mechanism across both disorders, and may be the basis of effective treatments for both.
effective treatments for SUD in schizophrenia may in part work by modulating brain reward circuitry dysfunctions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a better understanding of neurobiological mechanisms of treatment response will facilitate the development of new and more effective treatments for SUD in schizophrenia, which will improve patient outcomes.

the development and evaluation of treatments for SUD in schizophrenia would benefit greatly from a better understanding, and integration, of the neurobiologic mechanisms underlying the effectiveness, or ineffectiveness, of these treatments.
treatments that modulate brain reward circuitry may be particularly effective for SUDs among people with schizophrenia.
